pamphlet_excerpts: Different American Indian cultural areas: Pueblos were made of different types of materials (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 2: The Hopi and the Zuñi used stones that were mortared together and surfaced with plaster (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 3: Rio Grande Indians constructed their homes from adobe bricks of sun-dried earth mixed with straw (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 4: They stretched log beams across the roofs and covered them with poles, brush, and plaster (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Sometimes the beams projectedbeyond the walls and were used as pegs to hang food for drying (p. 7).
Step 2 (Different American Indian cultural areas): The women owned the apartments and all of the furnishings (p. 7).
Step 3 (Different American Indian cultural areas): In the centralplaza of the village, the people dug kivas, underground chamberswhere men conducted sacred rituals (p. 7).
Step 4 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Men also used the kivas asclubhouses, and women usually were not allowed to enter (p. 7).

pamphlet_excerpts: American Indian Tribe: An American Indian tribe, group: Using dugout canoes, Plateau tribes traveled and tradedwidely along the Columbia and Fraser river systems (p. 57).
American Indian Tribe Principle 2: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 2: From thewest came sea otter pelts and ornamental shells (p. 57).
American Indian Tribe Principle 3: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 3: Deerskins, hemp for basketmaking, and bitterroot were brought from theinterior (p. 57).

American Indian Tribe Principle 4: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 4: All sorts of goods changed hands: dried salmon, candlefish oil, baskets, carvings, even the canoes in which the traderscarried their wares (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (American Indian Tribe): Step 1 (An American Indian tribe, group): When horses came to the Plateau in theearly 18th c­ entury, tribes like the Yakima, Nez Perce, and Cayusebecame expert horse raisers and traders (p. 57).
Step 2 (American Indian Tribe): Step 2 (An American Indian tribe, group): The Plateau Indians had a complex system of beliefs andceremonies (p. 57).

Step 3 (American Indian Tribe): Step 3 (An American Indian tribe, group): Everyone sought visits from guardian spirits, andwhen someone felt they were about to be healed by their guardian spirit, there was a ceremony (p. 57).
Step 4 (American Indian Tribe): Step 4 (An American Indian tribe, group): Shamans had visions and appeared to the people in the guise of grizzly bears (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Learn Common Terms in An: Learn 10 Common Terms: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and revivingtheir arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 17).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 2: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 2: Many havechosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 17).
Learn Common Terms in An Principle 3: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in themodern world (p. 17).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 4: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part ofmodern society (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 1 (Learn 10 Common Terms): There is no easy answer, and no one knowswhat the future holds (p. 17).
Step 2 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 2 (Learn 10 Common Terms): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 17).
Step 3 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 3 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, livedcenturies ago (p. 17).

Step 4 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 4 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Others, like Geronimo, Ira Hayes, Ben Nighthorse Campbell, Ada Deer, and Wilma Mankiller, are people of the 20th and 21st centuries (p. 17).
